(with optative χρείη [it might be necessary], subjunctive χρῇ [it may be necessary], and imperfect ἐχρῆν or χρῆν [it was necessary], as the meter requires. Against the grammarians who considered χρή and δεῖ as adverbs, Apollonius argues in Bekker's Anecdota p. 538-542) it is necessary.
Specifically χρῆναι [to be necessary], i.e., to have to happen, is said of things that are established by fatal necessity.
The imperfect χρήν [it was necessary] meant 'it was necessary'.
in Clement of Alexandria p. 739, where δεῖ [it is necessary] stands for χρή [it is necessary] in Stobaeus, Florilegium 39, 14, who attributes this verse to Sophocles.

There are no examples of the disyllabic form ἐχρῆν [it was necessary] in Aeschylus. For in Choephori 907 ὃν δὲ χρὴν [whom it was necessary] is preferable to what is in M, ὃν δ᾽ ἐχρῆν [whom it was necessary].
